label: Feedback
summary: Feedback, in Maaike's work, is the input you receive from clients, editors, peers or reviewers on content you have created. It is a necessary part of content quality: without it, you cannot know whether your content meets its goals. Feedback requires both emotional resilience from the writer and a structured, critical approach to actually evaluate what is being said.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike treats feedback as something to be actively worked with rather than reacted to emotionally. Her first move is about detachment: separating your ego from your text so you can listen openly and take notes instead of getting defensive. Her second move is more analytical: she has a 5-point checklist for exploring feedback that covers facts, audience, stakeholders, required quality level, and whether the feedback itself is actually justified. That last point matters to her -- she is explicit that not all feedback deserves equal weight, and that part of professional judgment is knowing when a design decision is yours to make and defend.
open_questions: How do you decide in practice when feedback is not justified versus when you are simply being defensive -- Maaike raises both as possibilities but does not fully resolve the tension between them.
The checklist assumes you can schedule a proper meeting with the feedback-giver, but Maaike does not address what to do when that is not possible or when feedback arrives without context.
